claim: The worker posts to whatever callback URL a partner sets, and checks nothing about where it points.
notes: Stated outright, and the partner sets the URL itself.

claim: Nothing limits which outside addresses the worker may send webhooks to.
notes: The same stated fact as V1.3.6, read as a deployment control.

claim: Webhooks that carry download links go to http:// callback URLs as well as https:// ones.
notes: Stated outright: callback URLs can start with http://.

claim: Nothing states that the connections from the export API, the worker and the admin console to the queue, the registry and the stores are encrypted.
notes: The source says nobody has written it down. The submitter can state it, and the deployed setting also settles it.

claim: The description says nobody has written down how the services connect to the queue, the registry and the stores.
Nothing states how the export API, the worker and the admin console authenticate to the queue, the registry and the file store.
notes: The source says nobody has written it down. The worker's read of the order database is left out: the source states a database account for it, which answers how that connection authenticates. The account's reach over every brand is the question V8.4.1 holds.

claim: Every partner manager can read every partner's client secret back from the registry.
notes: Stated outright: the secrets are kept in plain text so a partner manager can read one back to a partner. V11.4.2 is left out because it governs user passwords, and V13.3.1 because it governs the backend secrets the application itself uses. A partner's client secret is neither, so this record holds the stated plain-text storage.

claim: Anyone who holds a signed download link gets the file for seven days with no token, and nothing states that the export API checks that a job belongs to the partner who asks for its status.
notes: The download half is stated outright: the file store serves the file to anyone who holds the link. The job-status half is silent and alone would be needs-code; the stated half settles the record. V14.2.1 is left out: the source does not say where the link carries its signature.

claim: Only the brand scope is stated as checked; whether a partner limited to orders can export customers is a hedge.
notes: One person thinks the check exists, and nobody has confirmed it.

claim: The worker reads every brand's tables with one account and exports the brand a job names without checking it against the partner's scopes.
notes: The export API checks the brand scope when the job is created, so the gap turns on who else can write to the queue, which is a permission grant.

claim: Exports of customer personal data stay in the file store for ever, with no expiry rule.
notes: Stated outright: nobody deletes finished files.

claim: Changes to a partner's scopes are not logged, and downloads of exports are not recorded anywhere.
The admin console can edit and delete any audit row.
The audit log is a table in the partner registry that the admin console writes, not a separate system.
Issued tokens are logged; nothing states that failed client ID and secret checks are logged.
notes: The source describes its logging in prose and names a row for each token issued. A fuller description can state whether failed checks are logged, and the code also settles it.

claim: Nothing limits how many exports a partner can ask for or how long the date range can be, and one worker takes jobs one at a time.
No control stops a partner from calling the export function without limit to pull bulk data.
notes: The same stated absence as V15.2.2, read as anti-automation against data exfiltration.

claim: One partner manager sets and widens a partner's scopes alone, and nothing states that a partner gets only the scopes it needs.
notes: The source states that one manager acts alone; whether managers keep scopes minimal is a practice to ask the team about.
